I dig @arthurbrooks's rules for breaking digital addiction:

• No phone for the first hour after waking and the last hour before bed

• Zero tolerance for phones in the bedroom and during meals, not even on the table

• Screen to grayscale and notifications kept to essentials

• Delete social media apps from your phone and check on a different device instead

• Check social media in 1-2 planned windows, maxing at 30–45 min/day

• Take four consecutive days off from devices each year, on retreat or vacay

Simple, perhaps even obvious, yet genuinely life-changing if you actually apply it.

candidates.text:
We contacted approximately 220,000 influencers to build Cal AI’s creator program.

People hear that number and assume we had a secret database.

We didn’t.

The real advantage was being willing to do an unreasonable amount of unglamorous work.

At our largest:
- 25 assistants worked on outreach
- Each targeted roughly 100 creators per day
- Around 2,000 emails could go out in a day
- Only a small percentage replied
- An even smaller percentage became partners

Influencer marketing looks creative from the outside.

At scale, it’s an operations problem.

Your results depend on:
- How quickly you identify creators
- How consistently you follow up
- How well you qualify them
- How effectively you build trust
- How disciplined you are about the numbers

Most brands don’t run out of creators.

They run out of patience and drive.

We didn't.

candidates.text:
not at all a good read. what is happening here is that both labs would clearly like to find a human proxy to give most of the credit to. they find it more palatable and somewhat less self promotional than saying “our swarm of machines has solved the historic problem and mathematics and soon many other academic fields are undergoing a chixculub event”. 

so they want to give Prof buckmaster lead authorship that, in any other situation, he probably would not be given, because it seems he had an excellent but not nearly complete solution (and the second part was harder if you measure by OOMs of test time compute, which is the language i understand). i understand less about this but it seems anthropic’s levent was trying to do this too, sending buckmaster a bunch of Claude proofs from an internal model. It’s just better vibes that way

openai is probably being overly generous about this and everyone involved seems to be bending over backwards trying to be noble and honorable. in reality, I doubt advanced mathematics will be considered a human dominated sport for much longer. these models are clearly superintelligent. they can do things the best people can’t do. I expect in the year to come you’ll get printouts of vast fields of famous problems being solved almost deterministically

candidates.text:
A museum put a one-star review on a T-shirt.

People paid to wear it.

The review: “Worst aquarium ever.”

The business: the New Bedford Whaling Museum.

Whale skeletons. No live whales.

The museum started selling the design in 2025.

This July, CBS covered the story. By the following afternoon, the museum had received 738 online orders, mostly for the “worst aquarium” merch.

What I love is that you don't have to care about whaling history to get the joke.

The shirt gives people a reason to be interested in the museum before they've ever visited.

That's a useful test for branded merch:

Would someone want to wear this if they'd never heard of your business?

Here are two ways to design a 20% off sale email.

Both are AI-generated concepts for the same fictional clothing brand.

A puts the discount front and center.
B gives the clothes more attention.

I'd test A as a sale reminder for people who already know the collection.

I'd test B when introducing the collection, so people can get a closer look at the outfit and fabric.

Before choosing fonts, colors, or a layout, I'd write down what readers should notice first.

For a sale reminder, my brief might say: “Make the 20% off offer the first thing people see.”

Neither concept has been tested.

What should people notice first in your next email?

It had half a billion users then and was the dominant market leader.

Instinct is valued at $2.5 Bn.

Could be less than 100 K users. 

Instinct will need to ‘grow’ into the valuation. 

Being a VC right now is high variance and intense competition. 

And, the SpaceX deal is re-liquefying venture coffers by $15 to $20 Bn alone…

We are seeing mid-cycle VC re-liquification and DPI. 

That’s going to keep the AI and cloud spend going, too. 

It’s pro-cyclical. 

Valuations are going to get even more insane in the AI space.
